q: The general formula of open-chain alkanes is:
x: Alkanes are saturated open-chain hydrocarbons with formula CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (e.g. CH₄, C₂H₆, C₃H₈). CₙH₂ₙ is the formula of alkenes and CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ that of alkynes.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is:
x: The longest chain has four carbons (butane) and numbering from the end nearer the branch puts the methyl on C-2. 3-methylbutane numbers from the wrong end, and the other two names miss the longest chain.

q: The correct IUPAC name of (CH₃)₃CCH₂CH₃ is:
x: The longest chain is four carbons, with two methyl groups on the same carbon. Numbering from the end nearer the branches gives locants 2,2, not 3,3. The other two names do not use the longest chain.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂CH(CH₂CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is:
x: Every longest chain through the branch point has five carbons, with an ethyl group on the middle carbon, C-3. 3-methylhexane has the same formula, C₇H₁₆, but is a different isomer.

q: A student names a compound "2-ethylbutane". The correct IUPAC name of this compound is:
x: Counting through the ethyl group gives a longer chain of five carbons with a methyl on C-3, so the compound is 3-methylpentane. An ethyl group on C-2 always means the longest chain was missed.

q: The correct IUPAC name of CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(C₂H₅)CH₂CH₂CH₃ is:
x: The six-carbon chain is numbered to give the lowest locants (2 and 3, not 4 and 5), and the substituents are written in alphabetical order, so ethyl comes before methyl.

q: The alkyl group (CH₃)₃C– is called:
x: In (CH₃)₃C– the carbon that attaches to the chain is bonded to three other carbons, so it is a tertiary (tert-) butyl group. Isobutyl is (CH₃)₂CHCH₂– and isopropyl is (CH₃)₂CH–.

q: How many structural isomers have the molecular formula C₅H₁₂?
x: C₅H₁₂ has three chain isomers: pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane. Other ways of drawing them are the same compounds.

q: Which of the following names is a correct IUPAC name?
x: 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane) is named correctly. 1-methylbutane is really pentane, 3-methylbutane should be 2-methylbutane, and 2,3,3-trimethylbutane should be numbered from the other end as 2,2,3-trimethylbutane.

q: The correct IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CHCH(CH₃)₂ is:
x: The longest chain is four carbons with one methyl on C-2 and one on C-3, so it is 2,3-dimethylbutane. 2,2-dimethylbutane would have both methyls on the same carbon.

q: A free radical is best described as:
o: An atom or group with an unpaired electron
A negative ion carrying a lone pair
A neutral molecule with all electrons paired
x: A free radical has an unpaired electron, which makes it very reactive, e.g. Cl• or CH₃•. A positively charged carbon species is a carbocation, not a radical.

q: Free radicals are produced when a covalent bond breaks by:
o: Heterolytic fission, one atom keeping both electrons
Ionisation of the molecule in water
Transfer of a proton to a base
Homolytic fission, each atom keeping one electron
x: In homolytic fission the shared pair splits evenly, so each fragment gets one electron and becomes a radical. Heterolytic fission gives ions (a cation and an anion) instead.

q: Which equation shows the initiation step in the chlorination of methane?
x: Initiation is the step that first makes radicals: UV light splits Cl₂ into two chlorine atoms. The reaction of Cl• with CH₄ is propagation, and CH₃• + Cl• combining is termination.

q: In the initiation step of methane chlorination, light breaks the Cl–Cl bond rather than a C–H bond because:
o: The Cl–Cl bond is highly polar
Chlorine pulls electrons out of methane
The Cl–Cl bond is weaker than the C–H bond
The C–H bond in methane is ionic
x: The Cl–Cl bond has a lower bond energy than C–H, so light of the right energy splits Cl₂ into atoms. The Cl–Cl bond is non-polar, and C–H is a covalent bond.

q: Which of the following is a termination step?
x: In termination two radicals join, so radicals are used up and none is formed. The two middle equations make a new radical (propagation), and splitting Cl₂ is initiation.

q: Which statement correctly describes a propagation step in a free-radical chain reaction?
o: Two radicals combine to form a stable molecule
A radical reacts with a molecule and a new radical is formed
A molecule is split into radicals by light
All the radicals present are used up
x: In propagation each step uses one radical and makes another, so the chain keeps going. Joining of two radicals is termination, and splitting a molecule by light is initiation.

q: In the chlorination of methane, one photon of light can lead to the formation of thousands of CH₃Cl molecules. This is because:
o: Each termination step produces two new radicals
A single photon splits thousands of Cl₂ molecules
Methane molecules also absorb the light and split
A chlorine radical is regenerated in each cycle of propagation
x: In propagation Cl• removes H from CH₄, and then CH₃• reacts with Cl₂ to give CH₃Cl and a fresh Cl•, so the cycle repeats many times. Termination removes radicals; it does not make them.

q: A mixture of methane and chlorine is kept in the dark at room temperature. What happens?
o: No reaction occurs, because no chlorine radicals are formed
x: Without light (or high temperature) the Cl–Cl bond is not broken, so the initiation step cannot happen and the chain reaction never starts.

q: When ethane is chlorinated in light, small amounts of butane are found among the products. Butane is formed in:
o: A termination step in which two ethyl radicals combine
The initiation step, when light splits ethane
A propagation step in which an ethyl radical attacks Cl₂
x: Two C₂H₅• radicals can join: C₂H₅• + C₂H₅• → C₄H₁₀. This is termination. When an ethyl radical attacks Cl₂ (propagation) the product is chloroethane, not butane.

q: The initiation step in the free-radical chlorination of an alkane needs:
o: An aqueous solution of the reactants
x: UV light (or diffused sunlight) supplies the energy to split Cl₂ into chlorine atoms. A nickel catalyst is used for adding hydrogen to alkenes, not for halogenating alkanes.

q: Methane reacts with an equal amount of chlorine in diffused sunlight. The main products are:
x: CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl. One H atom is substituted by Cl and the H joins Cl to give HCl. Ethane forms only in trace amounts by termination.

q: Which propagation step forms chloromethane in the chlorination of methane?
x: The methyl radical takes a Cl atom from Cl₂ and leaves a new Cl• to carry the chain on. CH₃• + Cl• also gives CH₃Cl, but that is a termination step. The last equation is the overall reaction, not a step.

q: To obtain mainly tetrachloromethane (CCl₄) from methane by free-radical chlorination, the conditions should include:
x: With excess chlorine, H atoms are replaced one after another: CH₃Cl → CH₂Cl₂ → CHCl₃ → CCl₄. Excess methane instead favours chloromethane, and darkness stops the reaction.

q: Ethane reacts with a limited amount of chlorine in UV light. The main organic product is:
x: C₂H₆ + Cl₂ → C₂H₅Cl + HCl by free-radical substitution of one H atom. Dichloroethanes need more chlorine, and the C–C bond is not broken, so chloromethane is not formed.

q: When chlorination of ethane goes on until two H atoms are replaced, how many structural isomers of C₂H₄Cl₂ can form?
x: The two Cl atoms can be on the same carbon (1,1-dichloroethane, CH₃CHCl₂) or on different carbons (1,2-dichloroethane, ClCH₂CH₂Cl). No other arrangement is possible.

q: What mass of chlorine is needed to convert 8 g of methane completely into tetrachloromethane? (C 12, H 1, Cl 35.5)
x: CH₄ + 4Cl₂ → CCl₄ + 4HCl. Moles of CH₄ = 8/16 = 0.5, so Cl₂ = 4 × 0.5 = 2 mol = 2 × 71 = 142 g. 284 g would be for 16 g of methane.

q: 16 g of methane is converted completely into chloromethane. What mass of CH₃Cl is formed? (C 12, H 1, Cl 35.5)
x: 16 g of CH₄ is 1 mol, which gives 1 mol of CH₃Cl. Molar mass of CH₃Cl = 12 + 3 + 35.5 = 50.5 g mol⁻¹, so 50.5 g forms.

q: The correct order of reactivity of the halogens towards methane in free-radical substitution is:
x: Reactivity falls down the group: fluorine reacts explosively, chlorine and bromine need light, and iodine hardly reacts at all with methane.

q: Traces of ethane are found in the products when methane is chlorinated. This is evidence that:
o: Methane loses H₂ to form ethane
Methyl radicals are present and can combine
Chlorine acts as a catalyst for joining methane molecules
x: Ethane forms when two CH₃• radicals meet in a termination step. Its presence supports the free-radical mechanism; carbocations are not involved.

q: Methane is chlorinated with excess chlorine in UV light. Which of the following is NOT expected among the products?
x: Successive substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄, with HCl at every step. Ethene, an unsaturated compound, is not formed in this substitution reaction.

q: Ethene is prepared in the laboratory from ethanol by heating it with:
x: Concentrated sulphuric acid removes a water molecule from ethanol at about 170 °C: CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O. Dilute acid at room temperature does not dehydrate ethanol.

q: Excess ethanol is heated with concentrated H₂SO₄ at about 140 °C instead of 170 °C. The main organic product is:
x: At the lower temperature with excess alcohol, two ethanol molecules lose one water molecule between them, giving diethyl ether (C₂H₅OC₂H₅). At about 170 °C with excess acid, ethene is the product.

q: Bromoethane is heated with alcoholic KOH. The organic product is:
x: Alcoholic KOH removes HBr from bromoethane (dehydrohalogenation): CH₃CH₂Br + KOH → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O. Aqueous KOH would instead substitute OH for Br and give ethanol.

q: In the dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide, the hydrogen atom that is removed comes from:
o: Any carbon of the chain, at random
The hydroxyl group of the alcohol solvent
The carbon next to the one carrying the halogen (β-carbon)
x: It is a β-elimination: X leaves from the α-carbon and H from the neighbouring β-carbon, so a double bond forms between these two carbons.

q: The ease of dehydration of alcohols with concentrated H₂SO₄ follows the order:
x: Tertiary alcohols lose water most easily and need the mildest conditions; primary alcohols such as ethanol need the strongest heating.

q: Butan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃, is dehydrated with concentrated H₂SO₄. The major product is:
x: By Saytzeff's rule, H is removed mainly from the β-carbon with fewer hydrogens, giving the more substituted alkene CH₃CH=CHCH₃. But-1-ene is the minor product, and 2-methylpropene would need a branched chain.

q: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, (CH₃)₃CBr, is heated with alcoholic KOH. The organic product is:
x: HBr is eliminated to give (CH₃)₂C=CH₂, 2-methylpropene; all three β-carbons are the same, so only this alkene forms. The alcohol would form with aqueous KOH, not alcoholic KOH.

q: Dehydration of ethanol and dehydrohalogenation of bromoethane are both examples of:
x: In both, a small molecule (H₂O or HBr) is removed from neighbouring carbons and a double bond forms. Addition is the reverse process.

q: Besides heating with concentrated H₂SO₄, ethanol can be dehydrated to ethene by passing its vapour over heated:
x: Hot alumina, Al₂O₃, acts as a dehydrating catalyst for ethanol vapour. Nickel and platinum are catalysts for adding hydrogen to alkenes, not for removing water.

q: 23 g of ethanol is completely dehydrated to ethene. What mass of ethene is formed? (C 12, H 1, O 16)
x: C₂H₅OH → C₂H₄ + H₂O. Moles of ethanol = 23/46 = 0.5, so 0.5 mol ethene = 0.5 × 28 = 14 g. 28 g would be for one whole mole of ethanol.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₂=CH₂ is:
x: Two carbons give the root "eth-" and the C=C double bond gives the suffix "-ene". Its common name is ethylene. Ethane has only single bonds and ethyne a triple bond.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH=CHCH₃ is:
x: The four-carbon chain has its double bond between C-2 and C-3 from either end, so it is but-2-ene. But-2-yne would contain a triple bond.

q: CH₂=CHCH₂CH₃ is named but-1-ene and not but-3-ene because:
o: Numbering always starts from the CH₃ end
The double bond is always placed at C-1
The name with the higher number is used for alkenes
The chain is numbered to give the double bond the lowest number
x: In alkenes the chain is numbered from the end nearer the double bond, so the C=C gets the lowest possible locant: 1, not 3.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₂=C(CH₃)CH₃ is:
x: The longest chain containing the double bond has three carbons with a methyl on C-2, so it is 2-methylpropene (2-methylprop-1-ene). But-1-ene is an unbranched isomer.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH=C(CH₃)CH₃ is:
x: The double bond is at C-2 from either end, so the tie is broken by giving the methyl the lower number: 2-methylbut-2-ene. 3-methylbut-1-ene is a different isomer.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH=CHCH(CH₃)CH₃ is:
x: Numbering from the left gives the double bond the lower locant (2, not 3); the methyl group then falls on C-4. Giving the methyl group the lower number does not take priority over the double bond.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₂=CH–CH=CH₂ is:
x: Two double bonds give the ending "-diene", with locants 1 and 3 and an "a" added to the root: buta-1,3-diene (1,3-butadiene). Buta-1,2-diene would have both double bonds on C-2.

q: Which molecular formula could belong to an open-chain alkene with one double bond?
x: Alkenes with one double bond have the formula CₙH₂ₙ, so with five carbons the formula is C₅H₁₀. C₅H₁₂ is an alkane and C₅H₈ fits an alkyne or diene.

q: How many open-chain alkenes have the molecular formula C₄H₈, counting structural isomers only (not geometric isomers)?
x: They are but-1-ene, but-2-ene and 2-methylpropene. Counting the cis and trans forms of but-2-ene separately would give 4, but the question asks for structural isomers only.

q: The group CH₂=CH– is commonly called:
x: CH₂=CH– is the vinyl group, ethenyl in IUPAC naming, as in vinyl chloride, CH₂=CHCl. Allyl is CH₂=CHCH₂– and ethyl CH₃CH₂– has no double bond.

q: Which of the following alkene names is a correct IUPAC name?
x: Pent-2-ene is correct. Pent-4-ene and pent-3-ene number from the wrong end (they are pent-1-ene and pent-2-ene). 2-ethylpropene misses the longest chain and is really 2-methylbut-1-ene.

q: The hybridisation of each carbon atom in ethene is:
x: Each carbon in ethene forms three σ bonds (two C–H and one C–C) using three sp² orbitals, and keeps one unhybridised 2p orbital for the π bond. Carbon in ethane is sp³ and in ethyne sp.

q: The bond angles around each carbon atom in ethene are about:
x: Three sp² orbitals lie in one plane, spread out as far apart as possible, about 120°. 109.5° is tetrahedral (sp³) and 180° is linear (sp).

q: The π bond in ethene is formed by:
o: Head-on overlap of two sp² orbitals
Overlap of the 2s orbitals of the two carbons
Overlap of an sp² orbital with a hydrogen 1s orbital
Sideways overlap of the unhybridised 2p orbitals of the two carbons
x: The 2p orbital left on each carbon is perpendicular to the plane; these overlap side by side to form the π bond. Head-on overlap of sp² orbitals forms the C–C σ bond.

q: How many sigma (σ) and pi (π) bonds are present in one molecule of propene, CH₂=CH–CH₃?
x: Propene has six C–H bonds and one C–C single bond (all σ) plus one C=C double bond (one σ and one π): 6 + 1 + 1 = 8 σ bonds and 1 π bond.

q: Which statement about the shape of the ethene molecule is correct?
o: The two CH₂ groups lie in planes at right angles
All six atoms lie in the same plane
The π electron cloud lies in the plane of the atoms
The molecule is tetrahedral around each carbon
x: Both carbons are sp² and the π overlap needs the p orbitals to be parallel, so the whole molecule is planar. The π electron cloud lies above and below that plane, not in it.

q: In ethene, the unhybridised 2p orbitals of the two carbon atoms, which form the π bond, are arranged:
o: In the plane of the molecule, pointing directly at each other
Parallel to each other and perpendicular to the plane of the molecule
At right angles to each other, one of them in the molecular plane
Along the directions of the C–H bonds
x: Each sp² carbon has its three hybrid orbitals in one plane, so the leftover 2p orbital stands perpendicular to it. The two parallel p orbitals overlap sideways above and below the plane. Orbitals pointing at each other would overlap head-on and form a σ bond.

q: Compared with the C–C bond in ethane, the C=C bond in ethene is:
x: The double bond (about 1.34 Å) holds the carbons closer than the single bond in ethane (about 1.54 Å), and needs more energy to break overall, although the π part alone is weaker than the σ part.

q: The π bond in ethene is weaker than the σ bond between the same carbons because:
o: The π bond contains only one electron
The π bond is formed from s orbitals
Sideways overlap of p orbitals is less effective than head-on overlap
The π electrons lie between the two nuclei
x: Side-by-side overlap of p orbitals is smaller than end-on overlap, so the π bond is weaker and breaks more easily. A π bond still holds two electrons, lying above and below the bond axis.

q: Ethene is attacked readily by electrophiles, while ethane is not. The main reason, based on the structure of ethene, is that:
o: Its carbon atoms are sp³ hybridised
Its C–H bonds are much weaker than those in ethane
Its π electrons lie above and below the molecular plane, exposed and loosely held
It has no electrons outside the plane of the molecule
x: The π electron cloud sits outside the plane of the nuclei and is less tightly held than σ electrons, so electron-seeking species (electrophiles) attack it. Ethane has only σ bonds.

q: Each C–H bond in ethene is formed by the overlap of:
o: An sp³ orbital of carbon with a 1s orbital of hydrogen
An sp² orbital of carbon with a 1s orbital of hydrogen
An unhybridised 2p orbital of carbon with a 1s orbital of hydrogen
An sp orbital of carbon with a 1s orbital of hydrogen
x: Two of the three sp² orbitals on each carbon overlap with hydrogen 1s orbitals to form σ C–H bonds. The unhybridised 2p orbital is kept for the π bond.

q: Ethene is bubbled through a red-brown solution of bromine in CCl₄, and the colour disappears. The product formed is:
x: Br₂ adds across the double bond, one Br on each carbon: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → BrCH₂CH₂Br. Loss of the bromine colour is the usual test for a C=C bond.

q: Ethene is converted to ethane by heating with hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst. The usual catalyst is:
x: Hydrogenation of alkenes uses finely divided Ni with heat (or Pt/Pd at room temperature): CH₂=CH₂ + H₂ → CH₃CH₃. Aluminium oxide is used to dehydrate alcohols.

q: The order of reactivity of hydrogen halides in addition to ethene is:
x: The H–I bond is the weakest, so HI gives up H⁺ to the double bond most easily, followed by HBr and then HCl.

q: Ethene is absorbed in cold concentrated H₂SO₄, and the product is then boiled with water. The final organic product is:
x: Ethene first adds H₂SO₄ to give ethyl hydrogen sulphate, CH₃CH₂OSO₃H, which is hydrolysed by boiling water to ethanol. The overall change is addition of water.

q: Ethene reacts with cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent). The organic product is:
x: Cold dilute KMnO₄ adds two OH groups across the double bond, giving HOCH₂CH₂OH. The purple colour disappears and a brown precipitate of MnO₂ forms, a test for unsaturation.

q: Ethene is treated with ozone and the ozonide is then broken down with zinc and water. The organic product is:
x: Ozonolysis cuts the C=C bond and each carbon becomes a C=O group. Each CH₂ end becomes HCHO, so one mole of ethene gives two moles of methanal.

q: An alkene gives only ethanal (CH₃CHO) on ozonolysis followed by Zn/H₂O. The alkene is:
x: Cutting CH₃CH=CHCH₃ at the double bond gives two identical CH₃CHO fragments. Propene would give methanal and ethanal, and 2-methylpropene would give methanal and propanone.

q: Polythene is made from ethene by:
o: Condensation polymerisation, with loss of water
x: Many ethene molecules join by opening their double bonds: n CH₂=CH₂ → (–CH₂–CH₂–)ₙ. Nothing is lost, so it is addition polymerisation, carried out at high pressure with a trace of oxygen.

q: What mass of bromine (Br₂) adds completely to 7 g of ethene? (C 12, H 1, Br 80)
x: Moles of C₂H₄ = 7/28 = 0.25; ratio 1 : 1 gives 0.25 mol Br₂ = 0.25 × 160 = 40 g. 20 g comes from wrongly using 80 g mol⁻¹ for Br₂.

q: In the addition of HBr to ethene, the species that first attacks the double bond is:
x: The electron-rich π bond attracts the electrophile H⁺, forming a carbocation, CH₃CH₂⁺, which Br⁻ then attacks. This is electrophilic addition.

q: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, reacts with HBr in the absence of peroxides. The major product is:
x: By Markovnikov's rule, H goes to the carbon that already has more hydrogens (the CH₂ end), giving the more stable secondary carbocation, so Br ends up on C-2. 1-bromopropane is the minor product.

q: In benzene, each carbon atom is hybridised as:
x: Each carbon forms three σ bonds (two to C, one to H) using three sp² hybrid orbitals. The remaining unhybridised 2p orbital takes part in the delocalised π system.

q: The benzene ring is flat, whereas the ring in cyclohexane (C₆H₁₂) is puckered. The reason is that in benzene:
o: Each carbon is sp³ hybridised, and its 109.5° bond angles fit a flat regular hexagon
Each carbon is sp hybridised, and its 180° bond angles hold the ring straight
Each carbon is sp² hybridised, and its 120° bond angles fit a flat regular hexagon
The π electrons lie in the plane of the ring and hold it flat
x: The interior angle of a regular hexagon is 120°, exactly the angle of sp² carbons, so benzene's ring is planar (with parallel p orbitals above and below it). Cyclohexane's sp³ carbons need about 109.5°, which a flat hexagon cannot give, so its ring puckers.

q: According to the molecular orbital treatment, the delocalised π electron cloud of benzene is formed by:
o: Head-on overlap of sp² orbitals of adjacent carbons
Overlap of carbon sp³ orbitals with hydrogen 1s orbitals
Sideways overlap of p orbitals in three separate, isolated pairs
Sideways overlap of six unhybridised 2p orbitals, one on each carbon
x: Each carbon has one unhybridised 2p orbital; all six are parallel and overlap sideways all round the ring, forming one continuous π cloud. Head-on overlap of sp² orbitals gives the σ framework, not the π cloud.

q: In benzene, the unhybridised p orbital on each carbon atom is oriented:
o: In the plane of the ring, pointing to its centre
Perpendicular to the plane of the ring
x: The three sp² orbitals lie in the plane of the ring at 120°, so the leftover p orbital stands perpendicular to that plane. This lets all six p orbitals lie parallel and overlap sideways.

q: The H–C–C bond angle in benzene is:
x: Every carbon is sp² hybridised with a trigonal planar arrangement, so all bond angles in benzene are 120°. 109.5° is the tetrahedral angle of sp³ carbon.

q: Which statement about the carbon–carbon bonds in benzene is correct?
o: They are alternately long single and short double bonds
All six are equal in length, between a C–C single and a C=C double bond
All six are the same length as the C=C bond in ethene
All six are the same length as the C–C bond in ethane
x: Because the π electrons are delocalised over the whole ring, all six C–C bonds are identical and of intermediate length (about 1.39 Å, between 1.54 Å and 1.34 Å). Alternating bonds would be expected only for a fixed Kekulé structure.

q: Which describes the shape of the benzene molecule?
o: A planar carbon ring with hydrogens above and below the plane
Planar hexagonal, with all twelve atoms in one plane
x: sp² carbons give a flat regular hexagon, and the hydrogens lie in the same plane, so all 12 atoms are coplanar. A puckered chair shape belongs to cyclohexane, whose carbons are sp³.

q: Which observation supports the idea that all C–C bonds in benzene are identical rather than alternately single and double?
o: Benzene burns with a smoky flame
Benzene has the molecular formula C₆H₆
Benzene is a liquid at room temperature
x: A fixed Kekulé structure would allow two different 1,2-isomers: one with the bromines across a single bond and one across a double bond. Only one ortho isomer is known, so all ring bonds must be equivalent.

q: In the molecular orbital picture of benzene, the delocalised π electron cloud lies:
o: As two ring-shaped clouds, one above and one below the plane of the ring
In the plane of the ring, between the carbon nuclei
As three separate π bonds between alternate pairs of carbons
At the centre of the ring, inside the hexagon
x: Sideways overlap of the six parallel p orbitals produces a continuous electron cloud shaped like two doughnuts, above and below the ring plane. The electron density between nuclei in the plane is the σ framework.

q: How many electrons are present in the delocalised π system of benzene?
x: Each of the six carbons contributes one electron from its unhybridised p orbital, giving six delocalised π electrons. Three would be the number of π bonds in a Kekulé structure, not the number of electrons.

q: In benzene, how many hybrid orbitals does each carbon use for σ bonding, and how many electrons does it contribute to the π system?
o: Three hybrid orbitals; one π electron
Three hybrid orbitals; two π electrons
Four hybrid orbitals; no π electron
Two hybrid orbitals; two π electrons
x: Carbon has four valence electrons: three go into the three sp² σ bonds (two C–C, one C–H), and one stays in the unhybridised p orbital. So each carbon gives one electron to the six-electron π cloud.

q: Resonance energy is defined as the difference in energy between:
o: The actual molecule (resonance hybrid) and its most stable contributing structure
The two Kekulé structures of benzene
Benzene and its products of combustion
Breaking all C–C bonds and all C–H bonds
x: Resonance energy measures the extra stability of the real, delocalised molecule compared with the most stable single structure that can be drawn for it. The two Kekulé structures have equal energy, so their difference is zero.

q: Resonance (contributing) structures of a molecule differ from one another only in the:
o: Positions of electrons (π bonds and lone pairs)
x: In resonance structures the nuclei stay in the same places; only the π electrons and lone pairs are drawn in different positions. Structures with atoms in different positions would be isomers, not resonance forms.

q: Which statement about the resonance hybrid of benzene is correct?
o: Benzene switches rapidly back and forth between the two Kekulé structures
Benzene is a 50 : 50 mixture of two Kekulé molecules
It is less stable than either Kekulé structure
It is one real structure, more stable than either Kekulé structure
x: The Kekulé structures are not real molecules; the actual benzene molecule is a single hybrid with delocalised electrons. Delocalisation lowers its energy, so it is more stable than any contributing structure.

q: The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol⁻¹ and that of benzene (to cyclohexane) is −208 kJ mol⁻¹. The resonance energy of benzene is:
x: Expected for three C=C bonds = 3 × 120 = 360 kJ mol⁻¹; actual = 208; resonance energy = 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹. Subtracting 120 from 208 (giving 88) ignores the three double bonds of a Kekulé structure.

q: If the enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol⁻¹, what value would be expected for a hypothetical cyclohexa-1,3,5-triene with three localised C=C bonds?
x: Each localised C=C bond should release about 120 kJ mol⁻¹ on hydrogenation, so three give 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹. The real value for benzene is much less negative because of resonance stabilisation.

q: The enthalpy of hydrogenation of cyclohexene is −120 kJ mol⁻¹ and the resonance energy of benzene is 150 kJ mol⁻¹. The actual enthalpy of hydrogenation of benzene is:
x: Expected value = 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹. Benzene is 150 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable, so it releases 150 less: −360 + 150 = −210 kJ mol⁻¹.

q: A large resonance energy shows that a molecule is:
o: Less stable than its contributing structures
Able to separate into its contributing structures
More stable than any of its contributing structures
x: Resonance energy is the stabilisation gained by delocalisation, so a large value means a more stable molecule. That is why benzene resists addition reactions that would destroy its delocalised system.

q: Benzene releases much less heat on hydrogenation than expected for three C=C bonds. This shows that:
o: Benzene is stabilised by delocalisation of its π electrons
Benzene has fewer than six π electrons
The hydrogenation of benzene is endothermic
Benzene's C–H bonds are weaker than those of alkenes
x: Less heat released means benzene starts at a lower energy than a Kekulé structure; the difference is its resonance energy from delocalised π electrons. Hydrogenation of benzene is still exothermic.

q: In the resonance hybrid of benzene, the bond order of each carbon–carbon bond is:
x: Each C–C bond is a single bond in one Kekulé structure and a double bond in the other, so in the hybrid its bond order is (1 + 2)/2 = 1.5. This matches the intermediate bond length.

q: Resonance is possible in a molecule only when:
o: The molecule contains only σ bonds
The atoms can move to new positions
Electrons can be delocalised through parallel p orbitals on adjacent atoms
Every carbon atom is sp³ hybridised
x: Delocalisation needs overlapping, parallel p orbitals on neighbouring atoms, as in benzene's planar ring. A molecule with only σ bonds or sp³ carbons has no π electrons to delocalise.

q: Which observation distinguishes ethene from benzene?
o: Benzene decolourises bromine water but ethene does not
Both decolourise bromine water at the same rate
Neither reacts with bromine under any conditions
Ethene decolourises bromine water at room temperature but benzene does not
x: Ethene adds bromine quickly across its C=C bond, removing the brown colour. Benzene does not add bromine under these conditions; it reacts with bromine only by substitution in the presence of a catalyst such as FeBr₃.

q: The characteristic reactions of alkanes, alkenes and benzene are, respectively:
o: Electrophilic addition, free-radical substitution, electrophilic substitution
Free-radical substitution, electrophilic addition, electrophilic substitution
Electrophilic substitution, electrophilic addition, free-radical substitution
Free-radical substitution, electrophilic substitution, electrophilic addition
x: Alkanes have no π electrons and react mainly by free-radical substitution (e.g. halogenation in light). Alkenes add electrophiles across C=C, while benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution, which keeps its aromatic ring.

q: Benzene usually undergoes substitution rather than addition because:
o: Benzene's C–H bonds are unusually weak
Addition needs nucleophiles, which benzene repels
Substitution keeps the stable delocalised π system, while addition destroys it
x: Addition would break the delocalised ring and lose the resonance energy. Substitution replaces a hydrogen and leaves the aromatic π system intact, so it is the favoured pathway.

q: When benzene is shaken with cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄ (Baeyer's reagent):
o: The purple colour disappears and ethane-1,2-diol forms
Benzoic acid and a brown precipitate form
The purple colour remains, as benzene is not oxidised
x: Baeyer's test is positive for alkenes, which are oxidised to diols. Benzene's stable ring is not attacked, so the purple colour stays.

q: Benzene reacts with electrophiles more readily than alkanes do because:
o: It has weaker C–H bonds than alkanes
Its π electron cloud is exposed above and below the ring and attracts electrophiles
Its carbon atoms are sp³ hybridised
x: Alkanes have only strong, non-polar σ bonds and no loosely held electrons, so electrophiles do not attack them. Benzene's delocalised π electrons are a site of electron density for electrophiles.

q: Benzene burns with a smoky (sooty) flame, while hexane burns with a cleaner flame. The reason is that benzene:
o: Has a much higher percentage of carbon by mass
Has fewer carbon atoms per molecule than hexane
x: Benzene (C₆H₆) is about 92% carbon by mass, compared with about 84% for hexane (C₆H₁₄), so combustion is incomplete and unburnt carbon forms soot. Both molecules have six carbons.

q: Which reagent reacts with ethene at room temperature without a catalyst, but reacts with benzene only in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst?
x: Bromine adds directly to ethene, but with benzene it needs FeBr₃ to form a strong electrophile and then substitutes. Hydrogen needs a metal catalyst for both, and steam needs an acid catalyst even with ethene.

q: Compound X (C₆H₁₂) decolourises bromine water. Compound Y (C₆H₆) does not, but reacts with Br₂/FeBr₃ releasing HBr. Compound Z (C₆H₁₄) reacts with Br₂ only in sunlight. X, Y and Z are:
o: Benzene, an alkene and an alkane
An alkane, benzene and an alkene
An alkene, an alkane and benzene
An alkene, benzene and an alkane
x: Decolourising bromine water (addition) shows an alkene; substitution with a Lewis acid catalyst and loss of HBr is typical of benzene; reaction only in light (free radicals) is typical of an alkane. The formulas C₆H₁₂, C₆H₆ and C₆H₁₄ agree.

q: Ethene reacts with bromine, and benzene reacts with bromine in the presence of FeBr₃. The organic products are, respectively:
x: Ethene adds Br₂ across its double bond to give CH₂BrCH₂Br. Benzene substitutes one hydrogen to give C₆H₅Br and HBr, keeping its aromatic ring.

q: Hot alkaline KMnO₄ oxidises methylbenzene to benzoic acid but leaves benzene unchanged. This shows that:
o: The ring is oxidised before the side chain
The benzene ring resists oxidation, while the alkyl side chain is oxidised
The methyl group makes the ring easier to oxidise
Benzene is more easily oxidised than alkanes
x: The stable aromatic ring survives strong oxidising agents, but the side chain attached to it is oxidised to –COOH. So methylbenzene gives C₆H₅COOH while benzene does not react.

q: Benzene is heated with hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst. The product is:
x: Catalytic hydrogenation adds three molecules of H₂ to benzene, giving cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂. The ring is not broken, so hexane is not formed.

q: Methylbenzene is heated with excess hydrogen over a nickel catalyst. The product is:
x: The aromatic ring adds three H₂ molecules while the methyl group is unchanged, giving C₆H₁₁CH₃ (methylcyclohexane). The ring stays six-membered and is not opened.

q: Benzene reacts with chlorine in bright sunlight, without any catalyst. The product is:
x: In sunlight benzene adds three molecules of Cl₂ to give C₆H₆Cl₆, an addition product. Chlorobenzene is the substitution product formed with Cl₂ and FeCl₃ in the dark.

q: Benzene hexachloride (gammexane), made by adding chlorine to benzene, has been used as:
x: One isomer of C₆H₆Cl₆, known as gammexane or lindane, is an insecticide. It is formed by the addition of chlorine to benzene in sunlight.

q: What volume of hydrogen at STP is needed to convert 0.5 mol of benzene completely into cyclohexane?
x: C₆H₆ + 3H₂ → C₆H₁₂, so 0.5 mol benzene needs 1.5 mol H₂ = 1.5 × 22.4 = 33.6 dm³. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 11.2 dm³.

q: What mass of chlorine is needed to convert 39 g of benzene completely into benzene hexachloride? (C = 12, H = 1, Cl = 35.5)
x: Moles of benzene = 39/78 = 0.5; C₆H₆ + 3Cl₂ → C₆H₆Cl₆ needs 1.5 mol Cl₂ = 1.5 × 71 = 106.5 g. Using 35.5 for Cl₂ instead of 71 gives 53.25 g.

q: Benzene reacts with ozone to form a triozonide which, on hydrolysis with zinc and water, gives:
x: Ozone adds across the three formal double bonds of benzene to form a triozonide. Hydrolysis breaks the ring into three molecules of glyoxal, OHC–CHO.

q: When benzene is converted into cyclohexane, the hybridisation of each carbon atom changes from:
x: In benzene each carbon is sp² (three σ bonds plus a p orbital). After adding hydrogen each carbon has four σ bonds and is sp³, as in any alkane.

q: Which equation represents an addition reaction of benzene?
x: In addition, atoms are added and nothing is removed, so the product has more hydrogen than benzene: cyclohexane, C₆H₁₂. The other equations replace a hydrogen atom and release a small molecule, so they are substitutions.

q: A hydrocarbon C₇H₈ adds 3 mol of H₂ on catalytic hydrogenation to give C₇H₁₄. It does not decolourise bromine water, and hot KMnO₄ oxidises it to benzoic acid. The hydrocarbon is:
x: An aromatic ring explains the three H₂ added without bromine water decolourising, and oxidation to C₆H₅COOH shows one side chain: C₆H₅CH₃. Cycloheptatriene is also C₇H₈ but its localised C=C bonds would decolourise bromine water.

q: In electrophilic substitution reactions, the benzene ring acts as:
o: An electron-poor species that is attacked by nucleophiles
An electron-rich species that is attacked by electrophiles
x: The delocalised π cloud makes benzene a source of electrons, so it is attacked by electron-seeking species (electrophiles) such as NO₂⁺ and Br⁺.

q: The intermediate formed when an electrophile attacks the benzene ring is:
o: An arenium ion (a carbocation, also called a σ-complex)
x: The electrophile uses two π electrons to form a σ bond to one ring carbon, leaving a positive charge on the ring: the arenium ion. A carbanion would carry a negative charge.

q: The rate-determining (slow) step in electrophilic substitution of benzene is:
o: Loss of H⁺ from the arenium ion
Combination of the lost H⁺ with a base
Attack of the electrophile on the ring to form the arenium ion
x: Forming the arenium ion breaks the aromatic π system, so it needs high activation energy and is slow. Loss of H⁺ restores aromaticity and is fast.

q: In the arenium ion, the ring carbon bonded to both the electrophile and a hydrogen atom is hybridised as:
x: That carbon now forms four σ bonds (two ring C, one H, one electrophile) and has no p orbital in the π system, so it is sp³. The other five ring carbons remain sp².

q: The arenium ion is less stable than benzene because:
o: Its delocalised π system no longer covers all six ring carbons
It has more π electrons than benzene
Its positive charge sits on one carbon only
It has lost a carbon atom from the ring
x: One ring carbon becomes sp³, so the remaining four π electrons are spread over only five carbons and aromatic stability is lost. The positive charge is in fact delocalised over three carbons, not one.

q: The correct order of steps in electrophilic substitution of benzene is:
o: Formation of arenium ion → formation of electrophile → loss of H⁺
Formation of electrophile → formation of arenium ion → loss of H⁺
Loss of H⁺ → formation of electrophile → formation of arenium ion
Formation of electrophile → loss of H⁺ → formation of arenium ion
x: First the reagents (often with a catalyst) generate the electrophile, which then attacks the ring to form the arenium ion. Finally a base removes H⁺ and the aromatic ring is restored.

q: In the bromination of benzene with Br₂/FeBr₃, the H⁺ lost in the final step combines with FeBr₄⁻ to give:
o: HBr and FeBr₃, so the catalyst is regenerated
x: FeBr₄⁻ formed in the first step gives up Br⁻, which takes the proton as HBr. This leaves FeBr₃, so the catalyst is not used up.

q: In the arenium ion, the positive charge is delocalised over:
o: Three carbons: the two ortho and the one para to the sp³ carbon
The two meta carbons and the sp³ carbon
x: Drawing the resonance structures of the arenium ion puts the positive charge on the carbons ortho and para to the sp³ carbon. The sp³ carbon has no p orbital, so it carries no share of the charge.

q: In the halogenation of benzene with chlorine, anhydrous FeCl₃ acts as:
o: A base that removes H⁺ in the first step
A Lewis acid that polarises Cl₂ to produce the electrophile Cl⁺
A source of Cl⁻ nucleophiles that attack the ring
x: FeCl₃ accepts an electron pair from chlorine, forming FeCl₄⁻ and the strong electrophile Cl⁺. Cl₂ alone is not electrophilic enough to attack the stable benzene ring.

q: The arenium ion could add a nucleophile (giving an addition product) or lose H⁺ (giving a substitution product). It loses H⁺ because:
o: No nucleophiles are ever present in the reaction mixture
H⁺ is the strongest electrophile present
Adding a nucleophile would form an sp-hybridised carbon
Loss of H⁺ restores the stable aromatic π system
x: Losing H⁺ lets the sp³ carbon become sp² again, rebuilding the six-electron delocalised ring and regaining resonance energy. Adding a nucleophile would give a non-aromatic, less stable product.

q: The nitrating mixture used for the nitration of benzene is:
x: Benzene is nitrated with a mixture of concentrated nitric and sulphuric acids. Sulphuric acid protonates nitric acid so that the nitronium ion forms.

q: The electrophile that attacks benzene during nitration is:
x: HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. The positively charged nitronium ion is the electrophile; nitrate and nitrite ions are negative and are not attracted to the π cloud.

q: Benzene is nitrated at about 50–55 °C. If the temperature is raised well above this, the main additional product is:
x: At higher temperature the nitrobenzene formed is nitrated again. The –NO₂ group is a meta director, so the second nitro group enters the 3-position, giving 1,3-dinitrobenzene.

q: In the sulphonation of benzene with fuming sulphuric acid (oleum), the electrophile is:
x: Fuming sulphuric acid contains dissolved SO₃, whose sulphur is strongly electron-deficient and attacks the ring, giving benzenesulphonic acid, C₆H₅SO₃H. HSO₄⁻ and SO₄²⁻ are negative ions, not electrophiles.

q: Which of these reactions of benzene is reversible?
o: Chlorination in the presence of FeCl₃
x: Benzenesulphonic acid loses its –SO₃H group when heated with steam or dilute acid, giving back benzene, so sulphonation is reversible. The other substitutions are not reversed in this way.

q: Benzene reacts with chloromethane in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The products are:
x: This is Friedel–Crafts alkylation: AlCl₃ produces the electrophile CH₃⁺, which substitutes a ring hydrogen. C₆H₆ + CH₃Cl → C₆H₅CH₃ + HCl.

q: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride (acetyl chloride, CH₃COCl) in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The organic product is:
x: In Friedel–Crafts acylation AlCl₃ produces the acylium ion CH₃CO⁺, which substitutes into the ring to give C₆H₅COCH₃ and HCl. Ethylbenzene would need an ethyl halide (alkylation).

q: Friedel–Crafts alkylation of benzene often gives some di- and trialkylated products, but acylation stops after one group enters. The reason is that:
o: Acyl chlorides are less reactive than alkyl chlorides
The alkyl group activates the ring, while the acyl group deactivates it
The acyl group activates the ring, while the alkyl group deactivates it
x: An alkyl group donates electrons, so the alkylbenzene product is more reactive than benzene and reacts again. An acyl group (–COR) withdraws electrons, making the product less reactive, so a second substitution does not occur easily.

q: Methylbenzene is treated with chlorine in bright sunlight at its boiling point, with no catalyst. The main monochloro product is:
x: Light and heat give free-radical substitution on the methyl side chain, producing C₆H₅CH₂Cl. With FeCl₃ in the dark, chlorine would instead substitute on the ring at the ortho and para positions.

q: 7.8 g of benzene is completely nitrated to nitrobenzene, C₆H₅NO₂. What mass of nitrobenzene is formed? (C = 12, H = 1, N = 14, O = 16)
x: Moles of benzene = 7.8/78 = 0.1; 1 : 1 ratio gives 0.1 mol C₆H₅NO₂ = 0.1 × 123 = 12.3 g. 123 g would be the mass from 1 mol, not 0.1 mol.

q: 15.6 g of benzene undergoes Friedel–Crafts acylation with CH₃COCl/AlCl₃ to give acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃, with a 50% yield. What mass of acetophenone is obtained? (C = 12, H = 1, O = 16)
x: Moles of benzene = 15.6/78 = 0.2; theoretical acetophenone = 0.2 × 120 = 24.0 g; 50% yield gives 12.0 g. Forgetting the yield gives 24.0 g.

q: Which of the following groups is meta-directing in electrophilic substitution of benzene?
x: The nitro group withdraws electrons and directs incoming electrophiles to the meta position. –CH₃, –OH and –Cl are all ortho/para directors.

q: Nitration of methylbenzene gives mainly:
x: The methyl group is an activating ortho/para director, so the nitro group enters mainly at the 2- and 4-positions (o- and p-nitrotoluene). The ring, not the side chain, is nitrated.

q: Chlorobenzene is nitrated more slowly than benzene, yet gives mainly ortho and para products. This is because chlorine:
o: Donates electrons inductively and withdraws them by resonance
Has no effect on the electron density of the ring
Withdraws electrons inductively but donates a lone pair by resonance to the ortho and para positions
Is a meta director that changes to ortho/para at high temperature
x: Chlorine's strong –I effect lowers the electron density of the whole ring, so it deactivates. Its lone pair, shared by resonance, raises electron density at the ortho and para positions, so those positions are still preferred.

q: Which order of reactivity towards nitration is correct?
x: –OH is a strong activator and –CH₃ a weaker one, so both are more reactive than benzene. –NO₂ is a strong deactivator, so nitrobenzene is the least reactive.

q: Benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH, is brominated with Br₂/FeBr₃. The main product is:
x: The –COOH group withdraws electrons from the ring and is a meta director, so bromine enters the 3-position. It also deactivates the ring, so the reaction is slower than with benzene.

q: Which route from benzene gives mainly 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene?
o: Nitrate first, then brominate with Br₂/FeBr₃
Brominate first with Br₂/FeBr₃, then nitrate
Treat with Br₂ and HNO₃ together in sunlight
Either order of nitration and bromination gives the same main product
x: After nitration, the –NO₂ group directs bromine to the meta position. If bromination came first, the ortho/para-directing bromine would send the nitro group mainly to the 2- and 4-positions.

q: Starting from methylbenzene, which sequence gives mainly 3-nitrobenzoic acid?
o: Oxidise with hot KMnO₄ first, then nitrate
Nitrate first, then oxidise with hot KMnO₄
x: Oxidation converts –CH₃ (ortho/para director) into –COOH (meta director); nitration then puts –NO₂ at the 3-position. Nitrating first would give 2- and 4-nitro products, which oxidise to 2- and 4-nitrobenzoic acids.

q: Which substituent activates the benzene ring towards electrophilic substitution?
x: The amino group donates its lone pair into the ring, increasing electron density, so it activates and directs ortho/para. –CHO, –COOH and –SO₃H withdraw electrons and are deactivating meta directors.

q: A –NO₂ group on benzene directs an incoming electrophile to the meta position because it:
o: Withdraws electron density most strongly from the ortho and para positions
Donates electrons specifically to the meta position
Increases electron density at the ortho and para positions
Blocks the ortho positions by its size alone
x: The nitro group pulls electrons out of the ring, and resonance shows the loss is greatest at the ortho and para positions. The meta positions are left relatively less electron-poor, so electrophiles attack there.

q: Which pair contains one ortho/para-directing group and one meta-directing group?
x: –OH is an ortho/para director and –CHO is a meta director. –CH₃ and –Cl are both ortho/para; –NO₂ and –COOH are both meta; –NH₂ and –OCH₃ are both ortho/para.

q: The general formula of open-chain alkynes containing one triple bond is:
x: An alkyne has two fewer hydrogens than the alkene with the same number of carbons, so the formula is CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (e.g. C₂H₂, C₃H₄). CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ is for alkanes and CₙH₂ₙ for alkenes.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃–C≡C–CH₃ is:
x: The chain has four carbons with the triple bond starting at carbon 2 from either end, so it is but-2-yne (common name dimethylacetylene). But-1-yne would have the triple bond at the end of the chain.

q: The IUPAC name of (CH₃)₂CH–C≡CH is:
x: The longest chain containing the triple bond has four carbons, numbered from the ≡CH end so the triple bond gets locant 1; the methyl group is then on carbon 3. Numbering from the other end (2-methylbut-3-yne) gives the triple bond a higher number, which is wrong.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂C≡CCH(CH₃)CH₃ is:
x: The main chain has six carbons and the triple bond is at carbon 3 from either end, so the tie is broken by giving the methyl group the lower number: 2-methylhex-3-yne. Hept-3-yne is the straight-chain isomer, a different compound.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₂=CH–C≡CH (vinylacetylene) is:
x: Either numbering gives the multiple bonds locants 1 and 3; when there is such a tie, the double bond gets the lower number, so the name is but-1-en-3-yne. The ending is always '-en-…-yne', never '-yn-…-ene'.

q: The IUPAC name of CH₃CH₂C≡CH is:
x: The chain has four carbons and is numbered from the end nearer the triple bond, so the triple bond starts at carbon 1: but-1-yne. Numbering from the other end (but-3-yne) gives a higher number, and the -ene ending is for a C=C bond.

q: The sigma bond between the two carbon atoms in ethyne is formed by the overlap of:
o: Unhybridised p orbitals side by side
An sp orbital and an s orbital
x: Each carbon in ethyne is sp hybridised, and head-on overlap of one sp orbital from each carbon gives the C–C σ bond. Side-by-side overlap of p orbitals forms the two π bonds; sp–s overlap forms the C–H bonds.

q: The common name of propyne, CH₃–C≡CH, is:
x: In common names alkynes are treated as derivatives of acetylene (ethyne); propyne is acetylene with one H replaced by CH₃, so it is methylacetylene. Dimethylacetylene is but-2-yne and ethylacetylene is but-1-yne.

q: In propyne, CH₃–C≡CH, the hybridisation of the carbons from the ≡CH end (carbon 1) to the CH₃ group (carbon 3) is:
x: Both triple-bonded carbons (carbons 1 and 2) are sp hybridised, while the CH₃ carbon has four single bonds and is sp³. Only carbons in a double bond are sp².

q: Which of the following alkyne names is correct according to IUPAC rules?
x: Pent-2-yne correctly gives the triple bond the lowest possible locant. Pent-4-yne and but-3-yne should be pent-1-yne and but-1-yne, and 2-methylbut-3-yne should be 3-methylbut-1-yne.

q: How many structural isomers that are alkynes have the formula C₅H₈?
x: They are pent-1-yne, pent-2-yne and 3-methylbut-1-yne. A methyl branch on carbon 2 of a four-carbon chain is not possible because that carbon is part of the triple bond and has no room for another group.

q: Alkynes can be prepared from vicinal dihalides by removing two molecules of hydrogen halide. This process is called:
x: Removing H and X from adjacent carbons is dehydrohalogenation, an elimination reaction; doing it twice gives a triple bond. Dehydration removes water, and hydrohalogenation is the reverse process (adding HX).

q: Which of the following is a vicinal dihalide?
x: In a vicinal dihalide the two halogens are on adjacent carbons, as in 1,2-dibromoethane. CH₃CHBr₂ and CH₃CBr₂CH₃ have both halogens on the same carbon (geminal), and 1,3-dibromopropane has them two carbons apart.

q: When 1,2-dibromoethane is heated with alcoholic KOH, the product of the first elimination step is:
x: The first molecule of HBr is removed to give bromoethene (vinyl bromide); removing a second HBr then gives ethyne. Ethane-1,2-diol would come from substitution with aqueous KOH.

q: In preparing ethyne from 1,2-dibromoethane, a stronger base such as sodamide (NaNH₂) is used to remove the second HBr from bromoethene. This is because:
o: The halogen in a vinyl halide is much less reactive than in an alkyl halide
Bromoethene is a gas and cannot react with KOH
Sodamide is a reducing agent that removes bromine
KOH would add across the triple bond as soon as it forms
x: The C–Br bond in a vinyl halide is attached to an sp² carbon and has partial double-bond character, so elimination of HBr from it is difficult and needs a very strong base like NaNH₂.

q: When 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane is heated with zinc dust, the organic product is:
x: Zinc removes all four bromine atoms as 2ZnBr₂ (dehalogenation): CHBr₂–CHBr₂ + 2Zn → HC≡CH + 2ZnBr₂. Removing only two bromines from a 1,2-dibromide with zinc would give an alkene instead.

q: 1,1-Dichloroethane (CH₃CHCl₂) is treated with alcoholic KOH followed by sodamide (NaNH₂). The final organic product is:
x: A geminal dihalide also loses two molecules of HCl on strong base treatment, giving ethyne. Ethanal would form from hydrolysis with aqueous alkali, not from elimination.

q: 18.8 g of 1,2-dibromoethane is completely converted into ethyne. What volume of ethyne is obtained at STP? (C = 12, H = 1, Br = 80)
x: M of C₂H₄Br₂ = 24 + 4 + 160 = 188, so moles = 18.8/188 = 0.1. One mole of dihalide gives one mole of C₂H₂, so volume = 0.1 × 22.4 = 2.24 dm³.

q: Which dihalide gives propyne on double dehydrohalogenation?
x: 1,2-Dibromopropane has bromines on adjacent carbons of a three-carbon chain, so removing two HBr gives CH₃C≡CH. 1,2-Dibromoethane gives ethyne, and 1,3-dibromopropane does not have its bromines on adjacent carbons.

q: In the dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide, the hydrogen and halogen atoms that are removed come from:
o: The base and the halogen only
x: This is a β-elimination: the halogen leaves from one carbon and a hydrogen leaves from the neighbouring (β) carbon, creating a π bond between them.

q: Alcoholic KOH, not aqueous KOH, is used to convert 1,2-dibromoethane into an unsaturated compound. The reason is that:
o: Aqueous KOH mainly replaces the halogens by OH groups, giving an alcohol
Alcoholic KOH is a weaker base than aqueous KOH
Aqueous KOH adds water across the multiple bond that forms
Ethanol acts as a catalyst that removes bromine atoms
x: In water, OH⁻ acts mainly as a nucleophile and substitution gives ethane-1,2-diol. In alcohol, the base is stronger and elimination is favoured, giving bromoethene and then ethyne.

q: Ethene can be converted into ethyne in two stages. Which sequence of reagents does this?
o: Br₂, then alcoholic KOH followed by NaNH₂
x: Adding Br₂ gives the vicinal dihalide CH₂BrCH₂Br, and double dehydrohalogenation then gives HC≡CH. HBr gives bromoethane, which on elimination only returns ethene; zinc removes both bromines and also gives back ethene.

q: The hydrogen of a terminal alkyne (≡C–H) is weakly acidic mainly because the carbon bearing it has:
o: No s character in its bonding orbital
x: An sp orbital is 50% s, so its electrons are held close to the nucleus; the carbon behaves as more electronegative, the C–H bond is polar and H⁺ can be removed.

q: The correct order of acidity of the C–H hydrogens is:
x: Acidity increases with s character of the carbon: sp (50%) > sp² (33%) > sp³ (25%). So ethyne is the most acidic and ethane the least.

q: When ethyne is passed over heated sodium metal, sodium acetylide forms. The gas given off is:
x: Sodium replaces the acidic hydrogen of ethyne, and the displaced hydrogen is set free: 2HC≡CH + 2Na → 2HC≡CNa + H₂. Ammonia is released when sodamide is used instead of sodium.

q: Ethyne gas is bubbled through ammoniacal silver nitrate solution. What is observed?
o: A red precipitate of copper(I) acetylide
A silver mirror on the tube walls
A white precipitate of silver acetylide
x: The acidic hydrogens of ethyne are replaced by silver, giving insoluble white silver acetylide (Ag–C≡C–Ag). A silver mirror is the Tollens' test result for aldehydes, not alkynes.

q: Ethyne reacts with ammoniacal copper(I) chloride (Cu₂Cl₂) to give:
o: A white precipitate of silver acetylide
A red precipitate of copper(I) acetylide
A green precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide
x: The terminal hydrogens are replaced by copper(I), forming red (reddish-brown) copper(I) acetylide, Cu–C≡C–Cu. This, like the silver test, is used to detect terminal alkynes.

q: Which reagent can distinguish but-1-yne from but-2-yne?
x: Only but-1-yne has an acidic ≡C–H hydrogen, so only it gives a white precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO₃. Both alkynes decolourise bromine water and KMnO₄ and both add hydrogen.

q: Which of the following does NOT give a precipitate with ammoniacal silver nitrate?
x: A precipitate needs a hydrogen on a triple-bonded carbon. In but-2-yne (CH₃C≡CCH₃) both triple-bonded carbons carry CH₃ groups, so there is no acidic hydrogen to replace.

q: 2.6 g of ethyne reacts completely with ammoniacal silver nitrate to form silver acetylide, Ag₂C₂. What mass of precipitate forms? (C = 12, H = 1, Ag = 108)
x: Moles of C₂H₂ = 2.6/26 = 0.1, giving 0.1 mol Ag₂C₂; M(Ag₂C₂) = 216 + 24 = 240, so mass = 24.0 g. 13.3 g comes from wrongly replacing only one hydrogen (AgC₂H).

q: In propyne, CH₃–C≡CH, the acidic hydrogen is:
o: Any one of the three on the CH₃ group
The one on the triple-bonded end carbon
None; propyne has no acidic hydrogen
x: Only the hydrogen on the sp-hybridised terminal carbon is acidic. The CH₃ hydrogens are on an sp³ carbon and are not removed by bases such as sodamide or ammoniacal AgNO₃.

q: Which statement correctly explains why ethyne is more acidic than ethene?
o: Ethyne has more π electrons, which push the hydrogen away
The C–H bond in ethyne is longer and weaker than in ethene
The sp carbon is more electronegative, so the C–H bond is more polar and the anion formed is more stable
Ethyne is an ionic compound that dissociates in water
x: Greater s character makes the sp carbon more electronegative; it holds the bonding pair closer, so H⁺ leaves more easily and the acetylide ion's lone pair, in an sp orbital, is more stable. The C–H bond in ethyne is actually shorter, and ethyne is covalent.

q: Ethyne is mixed with excess hydrogen and passed over heated nickel. The final product is:
x: With excess hydrogen and Ni, two molecules of H₂ add: HC≡CH → CH₂=CH₂ → CH₃CH₃. Ethene is only the intermediate.

q: Lindlar's catalyst is used in the hydrogenation of alkynes in order to:
o: Convert the alkyne completely to an alkane
Stop the reaction at the alkene stage
Add water across the triple bond
Add hydrogen halide across the triple bond
x: Lindlar's catalyst is a partly poisoned palladium catalyst; it is active enough to reduce the triple bond but not the double bond, so the reaction stops at the (cis) alkene.

q: Lindlar's catalyst consists of:
o: Palladium on CaCO₃ or BaSO₄, partly poisoned with a lead salt or quinoline
Finely divided nickel heated to about 250–300 °C
Mercury(II) sulphate in dilute sulphuric acid
x: Lindlar's catalyst is palladium deposited on calcium carbonate (or barium sulphate) and deactivated with lead acetate or quinoline. HgSO₄/H₂SO₄ is used for hydration, and AlCl₃ for Friedel–Crafts reactions.

q: But-2-yne is hydrogenated with one mole of H₂ using Lindlar's catalyst. The main product is:
x: Both hydrogen atoms add to the same side of the triple bond on the catalyst surface (syn addition), giving the cis alkene. Butane would form only with an active catalyst like Ni and excess H₂.

q: One mole of ethyne reacts with one mole of HBr. The product is:
x: Adding one HBr across the triple bond leaves a double bond, giving bromoethene (vinyl bromide). Bromoethane would come from ethene + HBr, and 1,2-dibromoethane from ethene + Br₂.

q: Ethyne reacts with two moles of HBr. The final product is:
x: The first HBr gives CH₂=CHBr. In the second addition Markovnikov's rule applies: H goes to the CH₂ carbon and Br to the carbon already holding Br, giving CH₃CHBr₂. 1,2-Dibromoethane is the common wrong answer.

q: Propyne reacts with one mole of HBr. The main product is:
x: By Markovnikov's rule, H adds to the terminal ≡CH carbon (which has more hydrogens) and Br to carbon 2, giving CH₃CBr=CH₂. 2-Bromopropane is the product from propene, not propyne.

q: Ethyne is passed into dilute sulphuric acid containing mercury(II) sulphate at about 75 °C. The final product is:
x: This is hydration: water adds across the triple bond, and the enol formed rearranges to ethanal, CH₃CHO. Ethanol is not formed because the product is a carbonyl compound, not an alcohol.

q: In the hydration of ethyne with dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄, the unstable intermediate that rearranges into the final product is:
x: Addition of H–OH to the triple bond gives ethenol, CH₂=CHOH, an enol. Enols are unstable and rearrange (tautomerise) to the carbonyl compound, here ethanal.

q: Propyne is hydrated using dilute H₂SO₄ and HgSO₄. The final product is:
x: Water adds by Markovnikov's rule: OH goes to carbon 2, giving the enol CH₃C(OH)=CH₂, which rearranges to the ketone CH₃COCH₃. Only ethyne gives an aldehyde on hydration; other alkynes give ketones.

q: What volume of hydrogen at STP is needed to convert 2.6 g of ethyne completely into ethane? (C = 12, H = 1)
x: Moles of C₂H₂ = 2.6/26 = 0.1; HC≡CH + 2H₂ → C₂H₆, so 0.2 mol H₂ is needed, i.e. 0.2 × 22.4 = 4.48 dm³. 2.24 dm³ is enough only to make ethene.

q: Saturated hydrocarbons such as methane mainly undergo:
x: Alkanes have only σ bonds and no π bond to add across, so they react by replacing hydrogen atoms with other atoms, e.g. chlorination of methane in sunlight.

q: The typical reactions of alkenes and alkynes are:
x: The loosely held π electrons of a double or triple bond attract electrophiles, and the reagent adds across the multiple bond. Free-radical substitution is typical of alkanes, and nucleophilic substitution of alkyl halides.

q: The reaction CH₄ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + HCl, carried out in diffused sunlight, is an example of:
x: Light splits Cl₂ into chlorine free radicals, which take part in a chain reaction that replaces a hydrogen of methane by chlorine. Two products form, as is typical of substitution.

q: The reaction C₆H₆ + Br₂ → C₆H₅Br + HBr, in the presence of FeBr₃, is classified as:
x: FeBr₃ generates the electrophile Br⁺, which replaces a hydrogen on the benzene ring. The ring keeps its delocalised π system, so this is substitution, not addition.

q: Although benzene is unsaturated, it usually prefers substitution to addition because:
o: Substitution keeps its stable delocalised π-electron system intact
Addition to benzene is impossible under any conditions
The C–H bonds of benzene are weaker than those of ethene
x: Addition would destroy the delocalised ring and lose the resonance (stabilisation) energy, while substitution keeps it. Benzene can undergo addition under harsh conditions (e.g. H₂/Ni or Cl₂ in sunlight), so addition is not impossible.

q: Which of the following is an addition reaction?
x: In the ethene + HBr reaction two molecules combine into one product and the π bond is lost. The hydroxide and nitration reactions are substitutions, and the loss of water from ethanol is an elimination.

q: Which statement about addition and substitution reactions is correct?
o: In an addition reaction a π bond breaks and two new σ bonds form
Addition reactions are typical of saturated compounds
A substitution reaction always increases the number of π bonds
In an addition reaction one reactant splits into two products
x: In addition, the reagent's atoms attach to the two carbons of the multiple bond, replacing one π bond with two σ bonds. Saturated compounds undergo substitution, and substitution does not change the number of π bonds.

q: Which of the following is NOT an addition reaction?
o: Hydration of ethyne with HgSO₄ and dilute H₂SO₄
x: Chlorination of methane replaces H by Cl and gives two products (CH₃Cl and HCl), so it is substitution. The other three reactions add a reagent across a π bond.

q: Benzene is treated with chlorine in bright sunlight without any catalyst. The product and type of reaction are:
x: In sunlight, three molecules of Cl₂ add to benzene by a free-radical route, giving benzene hexachloride C₆H₆Cl₆. With a FeCl₃ catalyst in the dark, substitution gives chlorobenzene instead.

q: In which reaction does the hybridisation of the reacting carbon atom stay the same?
x: In substitution of methane, carbon is sp³ before and after; only an H is replaced. In each addition the carbon changes (sp² → sp³ or sp → sp²) because π bonds are converted into σ bonds.
